title: Art Tatum's influence alongside Hines and Waller
summary: Wilson explains how he spent nights playing with Tatum, who showed him anything slowly, as a third influence after Earl Hines and Fats Waller records.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: And also, that was one of the best moves I ever made because I struck up a friendship with Art Tatum, because even though Art was only playing five o'clock in the afternoon, and a half hour a day on the radio, he loved to play -- he could play for 12 hours a day, and every night after I finished with Milt, I'd get together with Art, and we'd go to the after hour places, and different peoples homes, and friends of ours who had a piano, and the two of us, and visiting pianists would play until oh, nine o'clock in the morning, or noon -- as long as we could stay up and physically play the piano, we would take turns, and that was a very important point in my life, because Art

Tatum was a tremendous influence on me as a jazz pianist, because back in school, I had had the recordings of Earl Hines and the early Fats Waller solos, 'A Handful Of Keys' -- Fats Waller was doing the solos for Victor in the late twenties, and Earl Hines had begun to record with Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five. 'West End Blues', and all those things he did at that time.
And I had all those records, and I had never met Fats or Earl at that time, but I had learned the solos from the record, and I had already molded what I was doing at that time.

And then when I heard Art, that was the third big influence -- I incorporated what I could pick up from Art, and Art would show me anything I asked him to -- he'd slow it right down, and let me stand behind his shoulder, and he would show me exactly what he did.
Oh yeah. He was wonderful to me.
